messages.subject: Discrepancy between bilat.symmetry(RRPP = T) and bilat.symmetry(RRPP = F)
messages.subject_clean: Discrepancy between bilat.symmetry(RRPP = T) and bilat.symmetry(RRPP = F)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I recently came across some discrepancy using the bilat.symmetry function with and without RRPP. I’d like to clarify whether this may be a bug, or if there is some sense to be made out of it. The following lines of code provide a reproducible case (geomorph version 4.0.4, RRPP version 1.3.0):

#-------------------------------------------------------

library(geomorph)

data(lizards)

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = lizards$coords, ind = lizards$ind, replicate = lizards$rep)

liz.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 149)

liz.sym.noRRPP <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = T, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = F, iter = 149)

summary(liz.sym)

summary (liz.sym.noRRPP)

#---------------------------------------------------------

As can be noted, both ANOVAs have essentially identical results. However, Z values and P values do differ between liz.sym and liz.sym.noRRPP. That there is a difference is, I guess, to be expected, but P values for the inter-individual variation would seem to lead to entirely opposite conclusions. With RRPP, we find P = 0.54, while without it we have P = 0.0066.

Considering that the R squared value for inter-individual variation is 0.83, and that the variation explained by digitization error appears much smaller, I would personally be inclined to disregard the result using RRPP, and favor the one not using RRPP. More generally I’d be surprised to find a real biological dataset in which fluctuating asymmetry would be significant while inter-individual variation would not (but who knows?).

At the same time, the default behavior of the function is indeed to use RRPP for significance testing, which suggests to me that geomorph authors would tend to favor this option. If someone can confirm that the behavior of the function using RRPP is correct, I’d be interested to understand why this is the case, and how to deal with the interpretation of the results!

All the best

messages.body_plain:
This is not a discrepancy or error, it is a difference in how the permutations are performed.

RRPP is residual randomization from a reduced model. FRPP permutes the original data. While FRPP is the approach most folks are familiar with (i.e., ‘shuffle the data’), it has some statistical issues. Specifically, with factorial models (which bilateral symmetry evaluates) FRPP is known to produce elevated type I error and also have some issues with power.

Conceptually we know why. Permuting the original data conflates signal that should be attributed to the different effects in the model, and shuffles it across them. That is incorrect. The point of permutation is to generate empirical sampling distributions in such a way as to preserve exchangeability (first and second order specifically).

There is a very large literature on this topic both in the ecological context and also the morphometric and statistical world. The short answer is that RRPP is preferred.

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

messages.body_plain:
Dean’s point requires some clarification, I think.

There are two things at play.  First type I SSCPs are used, so the SS for ind would be the same whether using RRPP or FRPP, because the null model has just an intercept, meaning the null model for RRPP simply randomizes values when it randomizes residuals of the global mean.  One might posit that the result should be the same.

However, the second thing is that the F stat is calculated not with respect to residual variance, but the ind:replicate variance.  The distribution for the random SS for this effect will be quite different.  The null model for RRPP is ind + replicate, such that the ind:replicate effect is estimated with ind and replicate effects held constant.  The null model for FRPP is the global mean, meaning the ind and replicate effects are obliterated in every random permutation.

The large effect size with FRPP is misleading, because the SS for ind:replicate will tend to be small in every random permutation, simply because the SS for ind and the SS for replicate do not represent those effects in every random permutation. To be honest, FRPP is rather stupid in this case, just for this reason.

Trust the RRPP results, ignore the FRPP results, and take this point: a randomization test should not just be hapless randomization of data!  Every null model has exchangeable units under the null hypothesis, which are typically the residuals (but can be transformed residuals).  Only if a null model is just a mean does randomization of data make sense.  Yet, most permutation tests simply randomize data.  This can be dangerous, and your example sort of suggests why.

Having said this, I am a bit surprised by the large disparity between results, and will look to see if something could be amiss.

Mike

Hi everyone,

here is a good job opportunity for someone who would like to develop an own research initiative over a longer period of time. The maximum term for employment is six years as per university regulations. See text below!

Alex

Bonn Institute for Organismic Biology
An der Immenburg 1
53121 Bonn
Germany

Job Announcement
Scientific staff (f/m/d) at the Bonn Institute for Organismic Biology (BIOB), workgroup Blanke

Research at the Bonn Institute for Organismic Biology aims to increase our understanding of the phenotype of plants and animals, with the workgroup of Prof. Blanke focusing on form-function relationships in animals with different feeding modes. The workgroup Blanke would like to strengthen its team with a highly motivated applicant, ideally with a background in evolutionary morphology, biomechanics and/or imaging and with a doctoral degree either in the Biological Sciences, Engineering Sciences, or Computer Sciences.
Being a scientific staff position, the applicant principally can develop his own research initiative. Therefore, a particular emphasis will be placed on the applicants’ own ideas during the application process and how these can be studied (Ideally using a combination of both the applicants’ expertise and the expertise of the workgroup).
Applicants who are experts for other organisms besides insects should consider to apply since our approach includes comparative aspects on several taxonomic levels. We also welcome applications with a focus on methodological development in the fields of e.g. evolutionary modelling, geometric morphometrics, image analysis, biomechanics, or material testing of biological samples.

The position includes a teaching obligation of four semester hours (“Semesterwochenstunden”). Due to the teaching obligation, in particular within the Bachelor degrees in Biology, successful applicants will learn German up to the B2/C1 level within one year.

The position is paid according to the provisions of the collective agreement for the public service of the Länder (TV-L) within pay group 13 (100% working time). Experience levels are taken into account. Initially, the duration of the contract is 12 months. After a successful evaluation, the duration of the contract can be extended for another 24 up to 60 months depending on the WissZeitVG.

Apart from a full CV (Without photograph and without date of birth; Including own publications and contact details of 2 referees), applications should contain a letter of motivation detailing your previous research experience and an outline of your research plans for this position (1-2 pages max.). Please also state up to three publications from other workgroups which have considerably influenced your scientific thinking. While detailing your future research, please take into account that you can plan with a considerable research budget. Details will be communicated upon request, inquiries can be made with Alexander Blanke (bla...@uni-bonn.de).

The application (as a single pdf file) should be sent to the secretary of the IEZ (secr...@evolution.uni-bonn.de) with the reference number 1848-24. Applications which are sent to another email address will not be considered. The deadline for application is March 31st 2024, the estimated start date would be in May 2024. If no suitable candidate is found, the position is open beyond these dates. We regret that the state of North Rhine-Westphalia cannot cover application and travel costs.

Equal opportunities are important to us. The University of Bonn is committed to diversity and equal opportunity. It is certified as a family-friendly university and aims to increase the proportion of women employed in areas where women are under-represented and to promote their careers. To that end, it urges women with relevant qualifications to apply. Applications will be handled in accordance with the Landesgleichstellungsgesetz (State Equality Act). Applications from suitable candidates with a certified disability or equivalent status are particularly welcome.

We look forward to reading your application!

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

We are studying phylogenetic signal in dolphin vertebral morphology. We have a data set containing mean shapes for 24 species and we’re preforming both a PhyloPCA and a PACA. But we get a warning message (in red) at the end of the result when we call for the PACA results (see images).

We want to use this PACA to test for phylogenetical signal both on the Proc. coordinates and on the first axis of the PACA, but we are not sure what the message means.

If anyone could give us a hand, we would greatly appreciate it!

Thanks in advance

Dra. María Constanza (Kata) Marchesi

>

> Dear all,
>
> I recently came across some discrepancy using the bilat.symmetry function with and without RRPP. I’d like to clarify whether this may be a bug, or if there is some sense to be made out of it. The following lines of code provide a reproducible case (geomorph version 4.0.4, RRPP version 1.3.0):
>
> #-------------------------------------------------------
>
> library(geomorph)
>
> data(lizards)
>
> gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = lizards$coords, ind = lizards$ind, replicate = lizards$rep)
>
> liz.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 149)
>
> liz.sym.noRRPP <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = T, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = F, iter = 149)
>
> summary(liz.sym)
>
> summary (liz.sym.noRRPP)
>
> #---------------------------------------------------------
>
> As can be noted, both ANOVAs have essentially identical results. However, Z values and P values do differ between liz.sym and liz.sym.noRRPP. That there is a difference is, I guess, to be expected, but P values for the inter-individual variation would seem to lead to entirely opposite conclusions. With RRPP, we find P = 0.54, while without it we have P = 0.0066.
>
> Considering that the R squared value for inter-individual variation is 0.83, and that the variation explained by digitization error appears much smaller, I would personally be inclined to disregard the result using RRPP, and favor the one not using RRPP. More generally I’d be surprised to find a real biological dataset in which fluctuating asymmetry would be significant while inter-individual variation would not (but who knows?).
>
> At the same time, the default behavior of the function is indeed to use RRPP for significance testing, which suggests to me that geomorph authors would tend to favor this option. If someone can confirm that the behavior of the function using RRPP is correct, I’d be interested to understand why this is the case, and how to deal with the interpretation of the results!
>
> All the best
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi María,

Could you please provide more details?  Which versions of geomorph and RRPP are you using?  How many shape variables do you have, or how many landmarks and in 2 or 3 dimensions?

These warnings seem to be associated with the assignment of names to components, which are 23 for 24 species, but I am not sure and cannot investigate without more information.

I would be curious what would happen if you did the following:

1. PCA <- gm.prcomp(coords)
2. Y <- PCA$x[,1:3]
3. PACA <- gm.prcomp(Y, phy = myTree, align.to.phy = TRUE)

where myTree is whatever phylo object you use.  The reason for this request is to see if you get the same warning messages using fewer dimensions of data.

I would also be curious if the names of rows and columns from your original PACA make sense?  Check the $x object names.

Thanks!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Warning sign in PACA
messages.body_plain:
Hi María,

If you wish to measure phylogenetic signal and use an effect size based on the log-likelihood, you might want to trim the dimensions of the data, since you have more variables than observations.  Maybe try using the first 21 or 22 PAC scores (and be prepared to cull further), rather than the coordinates (can do this in the arguments, with PAC.no) or use a higher value for the tolerance (change tol in the arguments).  The warning is indicating that there were instances where NA values were found for the log-likelihood, caused by ill-conditioned residual covariance matrices, which are typical if they are near singular (always the case if variable number and observation number are about the same).

This is a difficult issue to anticipate and write a better warning for, but something we attempt to explain in the help file.  Because PACA concentrates phylogenetic signal in fewer dimensions than PCA, you can probably be reassured that using even a few dimensions is probably okay for your inferences about phylogenetic signal; i.e., if you repeat the analysis with say10, 11, 12, … maybe 20 PACs, you probably get similar z scores as results.  If it were me, I might explore what the results are with different numbers of PACs and find a place where the Z score seems stable but I do not risk bad log-likelihood estimated with too many PACs.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject_clean: Questions about generating asymmetrical components in bilat.symmetry
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph team,

I am trying to understand bilat.symmetry  a bit more by running through the R script (https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/blob/Stable/R/bilat.symmetry.r) and encounter some questions related to calculating. I hope I understand the script right. I used the data(scallops) as the sample data, which has a sample size of 5, and run the code from the help file as well. I have some questions:

1. I found that the difference between two sides calculated for scallop.sym$asym.shapes are asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[indsq,] - avg.side.symm[-indsq,]) (line 329). This is equivalent to (reflection - original) using the scallop data as indisq = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
However, the calculation of differences between sides for directional (DA) and fluctuating asymmetry (FA) are all based on (original - reflection). For example, the FA component is:
  FA.component <- ind.mns[-indsq,] - ind.mns[indsq,] #for scallop, it is basically (original - reflection).
  FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j)
  {t(matrix(FA.component[j,],k,p)) + mn.shape - mn.DA}))
(lines 341-343)

It would not impact ANOVA. However, it makes checking the relationship between scallops.shape$symm.shape, $asymm. shape, $FA.component, and $DA.component a bit confusing.
For example,  using the original bilat.symmtry(), I cannot get the asymmetrical shape of a specimen scallops.sym$asymm.shape[ , , 1] by using FA + DA + grand mean:
scallops.sym$FA.component[, , 1] + (DA.component[, , 1]  - DA.component[, , 2]),
#FA.componet = FA_residual + grand_mean
because FA is calculated from original - reflection, while asymmetry from reflection - original

I can obviously get the  $asymm.shape[ , , 1]  by  using the same way if I reverse the order of the reflection and original shapes so that asymmetric component beame (original - reflection):
asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[-indsq,] - avg.side.symm[indsq,])  #In the original function, -indsq and indisq are reversed

Are there any specific reasons for calculating only the overall asymmetrical component as reflection - original, but FA and DA as original - reflections?

2. Why are the asymmetric components directly calculated from the difference between the original and reflection shapes, rather than divided by 2? If we just do (original - reflection), would it calculate left & right difference twice?

Klingenberg 2015 <https://www.mdpi.com/2073-8994/7/2/843> pp. 865 also states that asymmetrical component should be original - symmetrical component, which is 1/2 of original - reflection, and DA = mean original - mean symmetrical = 1/2 * (mean original - mean reflection).

3. Why did the DA.component only export the mean original and reflected shapes? In that case, would it be more straight forward to just export a single DA shape as mn.DA + grand_mean? I feel users can able to calculate left and right mean shape by simply do a mean(asymm.shape).

Thank you very much for your time!

Chi Zhang

Instructional Assistant Professor,
Department of Biomedical Sciences,
Texas A&M University School of Dentistry, Dallas, TX

Dear Kata,

Regarding the $K.by.p results, make sure your choose verbose = TRUE in the function arguments.  That might not be abundantly clear in the help file, but the default is verbose = FALSE, which limits how many results to append to the object you make, to save memory.

Regarding the results, the two optimization methods could be quite different, and to be honest, this is an area that requires better research.  The “mean” option allows each shape variable to have separate lambda values and is optimized, variable by variable, finding the mean lambda as a summary statistic.  The burn option requires each variable to have the same lambda but seeks to find the value of lambda that produces the highest log-likelihood, before finding an effect size for that lambda.  These are essentially different approaches, so different results should be expected.  One has to decide beforehand whether variables can have independent optimizations or whether an attribute, like shape, has to have the same lambda for every variable.

Best,
Mike

> > > > > > > > > I recently came across some discrepancy using the bilat.symmetry function with and without RRPP. I’d like to clarify whether this may be a bug, or if there is some sense to be made out of it. The following lines of code provide a reproducible case (geomorph version 4.0.4, RRPP version 1.3.0):
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > #-------------------------------------------------------
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > library(geomorph)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > data(lizards)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = lizards$coords, ind = lizards$ind, replicate = lizards$rep)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > liz.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 149)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > liz.sym.noRRPP <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = T, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = F, iter = 149)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > summary(liz.sym)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > summary (liz.sym.noRRPP)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > #---------------------------------------------------------
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > As can be noted, both ANOVAs have essentially identical results. However, Z values and P values do differ between liz.sym and liz.sym.noRRPP. That there is a difference is, I guess, to be expected, but P values for the inter-individual variation would seem to lead to entirely opposite conclusions. With RRPP, we find P = 0.54, while without it we have P = 0.0066.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Considering that the R squared value for inter-individual variation is 0.83, and that the variation explained by digitization error appears much smaller, I would personally be inclined to disregard the result using RRPP, and favor the one not using RRPP. More generally I’d be surprised to find a real biological dataset in which fluctuating asymmetry would be significant while inter-individual variation would not (but who knows?).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > At the same time, the default behavior of the function is indeed to use RRPP for significance testing, which suggests to me that geomorph authors would tend to favor this option. If someone can confirm that the behavior of the function using RRPP is correct, I’d be interested to understand why this is the case, and how to deal with the interpretation of the results!
